title: Coupons at checkout: where a 'use' gets counted
head: feature/coupons

blocks.quote:
Apply coupon discounts at checkout and add a coupon API
POST /orders/:id/coupon takes a coupon code and attaches a discount to the order. Checkout charges the total minus the discount.

blocks.p: Two commits. One adds a `coupons` table and a service. The other wires an HTTP endpoint and changes the amount sent to the payment service.

steps.title: Say the intent before reading lines

blocks.p: Before opening any file, a senior puts the change into one sentence. A shopper types a code. The order remembers a discount. Checkout charges less. Each coupon works only `max_uses` times.
Who stops having a problem? Marketing can run a limited campaign, like "first 100 people get 500 yen off". The shopper pays less without support doing a manual refund.

This gives us a hypothesis to test: **one use of a coupon = one shopper who got the discount**. If the code counts something else, the campaign limit means something else. We will check that hypothesis against the code.
Note the risk profile. This touches money (the charged amount), a shared counter (uses), and a payment idempotency key. So most of our time will go there.

steps.title: Follow the request, including code that did not change

blocks.pre:
POST /orders/o1/coupon {code}
  server.ts readJson ─> handleApplyCoupon (400/404/409/410)
    CouponService.apply
      orders.get(o1)        status CART or PAYMENT_FAILED?
      coupons.get(code)     exists? not expired?
      coupons.consumeUse    UPDATE used_count+1 (atomic)
      orders.save           coupon_code, discount_amount

POST /orders/o1/checkout            (unchanged flow)
  OrderService.checkout
    save PENDING_PAYMENT
    payments.charge(total - discount, key="order-o1")  <- 1 line
    save PAID / PAYMENT_FAILED

reconcile batch (unchanged) ─> findCharge("order-o1")

blocks.p: Where we spend time: `CouponService.apply`, what a "use" means, and how the new amount meets the existing idempotency key. The key comes from code outside the diff (`paymentKeyFor`, `gateway.ts`).
Where we go fast: the test fixture edits that only add `discountAmount: 0`, the error classes, and the repository mapping. They are mechanical. We will check that they really are, then move on.

steps.title: The schema, and the line that makes the foreign key real

blocks.p: `discount_amount` is `INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0`. Existing orders get 0, so old orders keep charging the full total. That follows the repo rule: integer yen, never REAL.
A `REFERENCES` clause does nothing in SQLite unless foreign keys are switched on. So a senior looks for the place that turns them on. Here it is, outside the diff:

steps.title: The one line that changes money

blocks.p: This is the line that matters most for money. The senior question: if I revert it, does a test fail? Yes. This new test expects 2500 and would see 3000:
The test checks the outcome (the amount sent to the payment fake), not the internal calls. Its expected value is a literal `2500`. It is not computed with the same formula as the code. Good test.

steps.title: consumeUse: a check and a write in one statement

blocks.p: The obvious way is to read `used_count`, compare it in JS, then write `+1`. Two requests could both read 99 and both write 100, so 101 people get a 100-use coupon. Here the `WHERE used_count < max_uses` and the `+1` are one UPDATE, so the database decides.

This is the right design. It protects the limit with the database, not with steps in app code. Whether `result.changes` exists is Node's `node:sqlite` API, outside this repo. The use-limit test (`usedCount` stays 1) shows it working.
Order `o1` is in `CART`. Coupon `WELCOME` has `max_uses = 100` and `used_count = 0`. The shopper clicks "Apply" twice. Two `POST /orders/o1/coupon {"code":"WELCOME"}` arrive, one after the other.
What is `used_count` afterwards? And what if `max_uses` were 1, what does the second click return? Trace `apply` line by line.

steps.title: Answer: every apply is a use, even on the same order

blocks.p: The second request passes every check. The status is still `CART`, the coupon exists, and it is not expired. Nothing looks at `order.couponCode`. So line 28 runs `consumeUse` again. `used_count` becomes 2 for one shopper and one order.

head: Case
What happens
rows: 2nd call: 409 coupon_used_up, but the order already has it
A's use is never returned; order now has B
Script posts 100 times to one cart
Whole campaign used up by one client

blocks.p: So our hypothesis was wrong. In this code, a "use" means **one successful API call**, not one shopper who got the discount. There is no auth (true before this change too), so the last row needs no account.
Chapter in one sentence: the limit is enforced atomically, but what it counts is calls to apply, not orders that used the coupon.

steps.title: Must fix: make apply idempotent per order

blocks.p: The tests missed this because each test applies once per order. The use-limit test uses two different orders, `o1` and `o2`.

snippet.label: Fix idea (not in this repo)

blocks.p: Trace it with values. Same code twice: the 2nd call returns at the first line, so `used_count` stays 1. A then B: 409, and A keeps its one use. With `max_uses` 1, the 2nd click returns 200, not `coupon_used_up`.

What it does not prevent: two applies for the same order running truly at the same time. Both read `couponCode` as empty, and both consume. In one Node process with synchronous `node:sqlite`, apply has no real I/O between get and save, so they likely cannot interleave. That safety is an accident of the driver.

The sturdier version wraps `consumeUse` and an `UPDATE orders SET coupon_code = ? ... WHERE id = ? AND coupon_code IS NULL` in one BEGIN/COMMIT. If the order update changes 0 rows, roll back. That also fixes the gap where the use is consumed but `save` never runs.

steps.title: A declined card, then a coupon, then retry

blocks.p: `apply` accepts orders in `PAYMENT_FAILED`. Say `o1` was declined at 3000 yen. The shopper applies a 500-yen coupon and checks out again.
What exactly does the payment service receive on the retry? Look at how the idempotency key is built before you answer.
The retry sends `amount: 2500` with key `order-o1`. The first attempt sent `amount: 3000` with the same key. The key is built only from the order ID:

The comment says the service treats one key as one charge for 24 hours. Many payment APIs either reject a reused key with different parameters, or replay the first result. Which one this service does is outside the repo. So this is a **question**, not a must.

Before the change, the amount for one key never changed, so this question could not come up. The `PAYMENT_FAILED` condition was copied from checkout (orderService.ts:33). Ask whether it was chosen on purpose. Options: allow coupons only in `CART`, or include the amount in the key.

steps.title: Expiry: a broken date never expires

blocks.p: `expires_at` is free `TEXT` with no format check (002_add_coupons.sql:6). If someone inserts `2026/13/01` or `end of year`, `new Date(...)` is Invalid Date. Any comparison with Invalid Date is `false`, so line 27 never throws. A typo makes the coupon valid forever. That is failing open.

Time zones: `2026-12-31` (date only) is read as UTC midnight, which is 09:00 in Japan. A string without an offset, like `2026-12-31 23:59`, is read in the server's local time. A shop in Japan probably means the end of the day in JST.

Suggestion: `CHECK (expires_at GLOB '????-??-??T*Z')` or similar, plus a test at exactly `expiresAt == now`. Also a question: expiry is checked only in `apply`. A coupon applied on the 31st still discounts at checkout on the 2nd. Is that intended?

head: Weight
Finding
Where
rows: No DB CHECK on discount_amount (>= 0, <= total). The repo protects total_amount with a CHECK
Broken JSON body -> JSON.parse throws -> 500, not 400. No body size limit
Abandoned carts keep their use. Is a use counted at apply or at PAID?
No auth: anyone with an order ID can apply. Existed for checkout already
CouponService takes concrete SqliteCouponRepository; orders use an interface
Reused InvalidOrderStateError says "cannot be checked out"

blocks.p: The 404/409/410 responses tell a guesser whether a code exists. With no rate limit, codes can be enumerated. It is low weight unless codes are short.

steps.title: Things that look scary but are fine

list: Migration locks: SQLite's ADD COLUMN only changes the schema. It does not rewrite the table. Migrations run in one transaction at startup (db.ts:17-25).
Rollback: old code ignores the new columns, so it would charge the full total. That is safe for the shop, but annoying for shoppers who applied a coupon. Easy to undo.
Scale: a few primary-key lookups per request. No loops, no unbounded reads.
Test edits in 3 files: only `discountAmount: 0` was added. No expected value changed. No test was removed or skipped.
`Math.min(discount, total)` keeps the charge >= 0. Nothing in this repo changes `totalAmount` after apply, so the cap cannot go stale today.
apply vs checkout race: while checkout awaits the payment call, the order is `PENDING_PAYMENT`, so apply returns 409.

blocks.p: Each item was checked in the files named. The race item is inferred from the code's await points, not from running it.

steps.title: Did it make the codebase better?

blocks.p: Mostly yes. The structure follows the repo: integer yen, an atomic counter, a working foreign key, and a tested charge line. But one hole changes what the business limit means. A must fix, then merge.

list: **Must**: `apply` consumes a use on every call, including repeats on the same order. Return early for the same code, reject a different code, and add a test that applies twice to one order.
**Question**: In `PAYMENT_FAILED`, a coupon changes the amount under the same idempotency key `order-<id>`. What does the payment service do with that? If unsure, allow coupons only in `CART`.
**Suggestion**: Validate `expires_at` format and time zone. An Invalid Date never expires.
**Good**: The single conditional UPDATE in `consumeUse` keeps the limit safe under concurrency without any locking code.
Write the intent as a hypothesis ("one use = one shopper") and test it against the code. Here the hypothesis was wrong.
Look outside the diff: `PRAGMA foreign_keys`, `paymentKeyFor`, the gateway comment.
Feed concrete inputs: a double click, two different codes, a broken date, a declined then retried order.
Ask "if I revert this line, which test fails?" for the money line.
Weigh each finding: must, question (external spec), suggestion, nit. Also say what is fine and why.
Check that a fix really works by tracing values, and say what it still does not cover.
